title: New Amsterdam, One-Shotted by Opus 5
author: dvdhutch
selftext:
Welcome to New Amsterdam, traveler! It is the year 1660 and you've just stepped foot on to the southern tip of what would become Manhattan.

My one-shot game! I came across [this post](https://x.com/levelsio/status/2081339304752640137) by X/levelsio building New Amsterdam w/ Opus 5, so decided to take a stab at it.

After detailing how I wanted a realistic + historically accurate New Amsterdam, I provided a sub-agent loop ([original prompt here](https://github.com/mshumer/Claude-of-Duty/blob/main/prompt.md), borrowed from [mattshumer\_](https://x.com/mattshumer_)) to Opus 5 by in Cursor.

I'm big history buff for this period, so it was fun to see how accurate it turned out!

I fed Opus one of my fav books on the period ([The Island at the Center of the World](https://www.amazon.com/Island-Center-World-Manhattan-Forgotten/dp/1400078679)) and instructed it to go wild on the [New Netherland Archive](https://www.archives.gov/nhprc/projects/catalog/new-netherland-archive) (\~7k pages of original records from the New Netherland Colony).

This set the map + setting.

Then, the loop-based sub-agents referenced general Assassin's Creed-style game mechanics (but first-person POV).  
  
Added it as a skill in Cursor, so super easy to /game-loop it in.

I think the main difference between original I came across and my attempt was I just left the agent running for a really long time, so while it was 'one-shot' it takes a RLY long time to run. Not bad for a first pass.

replies.author: dvdhutch
replies.body:
Here's the game-loop prompt I used, which adapts Matt's:

    I want you to build a [game_idea] at the level of the most recent [reference] games. It should be utterly perfect, visually beautiful, with every single thing done at AAA quality—from textures to physics to anything you could think of.
    
    Fan out sub-agents and have sub-agents tackle each one individually so that the game is utterly perfect. You should /loop on each item and have a separate sub-agent check it visually to ensure it looks triple A. That separate sub-agent should be a really harsh critic, and if it doesn't look triple A, it should keep going.
    Don't stop until each sub-agent is utterly wowed with the quality when compared with the actual [reference] game. It should literally compare them side by side blind and say which one looks better. Do this in ThreeJS. /loop until it's utterly perfect. Fan out sub-agents and ultracode.
    
    [game_idea] = the proposed game by the user
    
    [reference] = find a notable comparison to the user suggested game. if the game idea is more specific, or perhaps a combination of a few already existing game ideas, pull a few titles into this as reference, separated by commas. do not exceed three titles. you must reference at least one title.

For `game_idea` I put down the above info about New Netherland and told it to do its own research, but steered it to the listed sources. And then `reference` just briefly mentioned that I wanted the general gameplay to follow AC-style mechanics (didn't really get to that in this first pass).

All told, took \~50 mins, and burned about that much in tokens on Cursor (\~$50).

replies.author: dvdhutch
replies.body:
You can think of it like one agent directing a handful of other agents to do tasks. 

It's useful for this because what would typically take each agent a long time can run in parallel, and the 'head' agent can check in on the work!

Cursor has a nice definition here: [https://cursor.com/docs/subagents](https://cursor.com/docs/subagents)

I think building more projects will help you figure out what it actually means to use a subagent in a real project (just multiple things happening at once).

replies.author: dvdhutch

Depends on what your goals are; in this case I wanted to see what the frontier of 3D environments would look like for models.

But for a lot of other games, you can do a lot more with less, e.g. Kimi K3 (Moonshot) is going to be really lightweight and get you a lot of bang for your buck, particularly if you don't want 3D.

But yeah in this case, since they're instructed to reflect on their work and *only* stop once it's deemed satisfactory, could be long long time.

comments.author: clonicle
comments.body:
Just a few questions on running a one-shot like this. It looks like a great start, but how the game works as a product is another animal in the end.

* Any idea how the assets are created in-game?
* Were they individually textured, or were trim-sheets used?
* Is the lighting baked or dynamic at runtime?
* What engine is the client?
* Hows the FPS?

My questions are NOT being critical of your one-shot, it looks great. I'm curious how the nuts-and-bolts are aligned so when you have 50x more assets, will the FPS grind to a halt or remain smooth.

replies.author: dvdhutch
replies.body:
Thanks for asking, those are all good questions! I specifically narrowed the scope of this to focus on the map and mechanics before actual making any gameplay.

* There are actually zero assets! All procedurally generated
* As such, not textured nor trim-sheets, but tiles (Opus is quite good at this but if you look carefully there are clearly strange gaps in places, e.g building roofs)
* Lighting is dynamic
* Custom WebGL client on Three.js
* FPS was \~60ish on my laptop (M3 MacBook)

replies.author: clonicle
replies.body:
I'm diving into the weeds and that might not be appropriate, sorry. If this is going to be a multiplayer game, you're going to face the hurdle of replication. Currently, the standard is to have the client handle the rendering and leverage local assets. Character actions and telemetry, etc are communicated with the server and across to all other clients participating in the game. This is why I was asking the questions above. 

As I read your answers, I think this would work well as a prototype/proof-of-concept for laying out a city. But you may run into real issues when you have to handle how that data gets replicated across all clients.

Part of this may just be a wording issue too. When I hear one-shot, I am expecting a production-ready game. I don't see that yet. I think you have a very good proof-of-concept going that you can build upon. You accomplished more in that one prompt than teams were able to do at much more expensive rates. You've got a great start and what looks like a clear vision, but the work is just starting.

Note: I may be completely wrong too. I have not played Claude of Duty, nor built for it. Maybe what you have will be just fine. I have been working in Unreal which is its own circus. I assume the fundamentals are similar though.

replies.author: dvdhutch
replies.body:
No worries! This was a fun proof of concept, admittedly saw the Opus one-shot hype and wanted to see if it was legit. I did harbor some doubts as to if the others were authentically made in one go, so this was a fun experiment to verify that it is doable. Took about an hour out of my day, and that was it.

Def not pursuing multiplayer nor commercial for this project, but I appreciate the heads up!

Good points: yes to Three.js, no blender at all used. All assets were procedurally generated w/ Opus 5. Relatedly: some others in this thread mentioned how Claude struggled w/ Blender, and I've also found this to be the case. Seems like because Opus 5 is trained on HTML it's much better at this approach (procedural generation).

Here's the repo! [https://github.com/dvdhutch/New-Amsterdam](https://github.com/dvdhutch/New-Amsterdam)
